findings.title: Policy exists but lets one user reach another user's rows
findings.evidence: RLS probe on `public.patients`: user B could select 1 of 1 of user A's rows. Let through by policy "Clinic staff can view patients" (select, `using (auth.role() = 'authenticated'::text)`).
findings.snippet:
15 | create policy "Clinic staff can view patients"
  16 |   on public.patients for select
  17 |   to authenticated
  18 |   using (auth.role() = 'authenticated');
findings.whyItMatters: The table has Row Level Security and policies, so a dashboard check passes. The probe signed in as a second user and still read or changed the first user's rows: the policy checks that someone is signed in, not who owns the row.
findings.fix: Compare the owner column with `auth.uid()` in every policy on this table (`using` for reads, updates and deletes, `with check` for inserts and updates).
findings.subject: public.patients

patch.diff:
diff --git a/supabase/migrations/20261116090000_scope_policies_patients.sql b/supabase/migrations/20261116090000_scope_policies_patients.sql
new file mode 100644
--- /dev/null
+++ b/supabase/migrations/20261116090000_scope_policies_patients.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,8 @@
+-- PA-01: tie public.patients policies to the row owner.
+-- Generated by prelaunch-audit. Review before applying.
+drop policy if exists "Clinic staff can view patients" on public.patients;
+
+create policy "Clinic staff can view patients"
+  on public.patients for select
+  to authenticated
+  using ((select auth.uid()) = clinician_id);
patch.summary: Rewrites "Clinic staff can view patients" so clinician_id must equal the signed-in user's id. The names stay, so nothing else that refers to them breaks.
caveats: Check that this is who should have access. If a team or shared workspace should see the rows too, scope the policy to that membership instead.

findings.title: View skips Row Level Security
findings.evidence: View `public.todays_schedule` has no `security_invoker`, so it reads the tables below it without RLS.
findings.snippet:
23 | create view public.todays_schedule as
  24 |   select a.id, a.scheduled_at, a.reason, p.full_name, p.date_of_birth, p.clinician_id
  25 |     from public.appointments a
  26 |     join public.patients p on p.id = a.patient_id
findings.whyItMatters: Postgres views run with the rights of whoever created them, so they ignore the policies of the tables below. Supabase serves the view over the API, which gives every caller the rows your policies were meant to hide.
findings.fix: Set `security_invoker = true` on the view (Postgres 15+), so it runs with the caller's rights and the table policies apply.
findings.subject: public.todays_schedule

patch.diff:
diff --git a/supabase/migrations/20261116090001_security_invoker_todays_schedule.sql b/supabase/migrations/20261116090001_security_invoker_todays_schedule.sql
new file mode 100644
--- /dev/null
+++ b/supabase/migrations/20261116090001_security_invoker_todays_schedule.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,3 @@
+-- PA-02: make public.todays_schedule respect the caller's RLS.
+-- Generated by prelaunch-audit. Review before applying.
+alter view public.todays_schedule set (security_invoker = true);
patch.summary: Sets security_invoker on public.todays_schedule, so the policies of the tables below it apply to whoever queries it.
caveats: Needs Postgres 15 or newer (every current Supabase project is).

findings.title: Health files in a public storage bucket

cwe.name: Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties

findings.evidence: Storage bucket `lab-results` is public and its name says it holds health records, and `src/lib/labs.ts` uploads patient files to it.
findings.snippet:
1 | insert into storage.buckets (id, name, public)
   2 | values ('lab-results', 'lab-results', true);
findings.whyItMatters: Every file in a public bucket opens for anyone who has its address, with no sign-in. Supabase's own HIPAA checklist says not to keep health data in public buckets. Lab results and scans with a predictable path are one guess away.
findings.fix: Make the bucket private, limit reads to the owner's folder with a policy on `storage.objects`, and show files through short-lived signed URLs created after checking who is asking.
findings.subject: lab-results

+update storage.buckets set public = false where id = 'lab-results';
patch.summary: Makes the lab-results bucket private. Files stay where they are.

findings.title: Table with health data has no migration
findings.evidence: `public.intake_forms` is in the generated types with `allergies`, `symptoms`, but no migration creates it or sets its policies.
findings.whyItMatters: The app's generated types show this table, so it exists on the live project, but no migration in the repo creates it or sets its policies. It was most likely made in the Supabase dashboard. Nobody reviewing the code can tell who may read these health records, and the RLS probe could not try it.
findings.fix: Run `supabase db pull` to get the table and its policies into a migration, check that every policy compares the owner with `auth.uid()`, and run this audit again (or with --live) to test it.
findings.subject: public.intake_forms

findings.title: Session replay records pages that show health data

cwe.name: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

findings.evidence: PostHog loads on every page and can record the screen, including `src/pages/PatientDetail.tsx`, `src/pages/Patients.tsx`, which show `reason`, `clinical_notes`, `diagnosis`, `insurance_member_id`, `date_of_birth`, `mrn`.
findings.whyItMatters: A session replay script copies what is on the screen (text, form fields, clicks) to the vendor's servers so you can watch visits back. On these pages that is patients' health data. Under HIPAA the vendor then needs a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA), and many analytics vendors do not sign one for every plan.
findings.fix: Do not load the script on pages that show health data (or at all in the logged-in app). If you keep it, use a plan for which the vendor signs a BAA, sign it, and turn on masking of all text and inputs.
findings.subject: PostHog

patch.summary: Turns session recording off in the PostHog init, whatever the project setting says.
caveats: PostHog still gets page views and autocaptured clicks, which can include text from the page. Set `autocapture: false` and stop capturing on the logged-in pages unless PostHog signs a BAA with you.

findings.title: Health data sent to a vendor that must sign a BAA

cwe.name: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

findings.evidence: `supabase/functions/send-reminder/index.ts` reads `public.appointments`, `public.patients` and calls Resend; the code handles `reason`, `date_of_birth`.
findings.whyItMatters: This server code reads health records and sends a request to an outside API (AI, email or SMS). Under HIPAA that vendor is a business associate: without a signed BAA for the exact product you call, sending it patient data is a disclosure the law does not allow, whatever the vendor's own security.
findings.fix: Check whether the vendor signs a BAA for this API, sign it before launch, and send only the fields the call needs. Where there is no BAA, send no patient fields (for email and SMS: 'You have a new message, sign in to read it').
findings.subject: Resend (supabase/functions/send-reminder/index.ts)

findings.title: Third-party script on pages that show health data

cwe.name: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

findings.evidence: Google Analytics loads on every page, including `src/pages/PatientDetail.tsx`, `src/pages/Patients.tsx`, which show `reason`, `clinical_notes`, `diagnosis`, `insurance_member_id`, `date_of_birth`, `mrn`.
findings.whyItMatters: The script runs with full access to every page it loads on and sends page addresses and events to its vendor. On pages with health data, an address like /patients/<id> or an event with a field value already says something about a patient, which HIPAA counts as health information.
findings.fix: Load analytics only on the public marketing pages, not in the logged-in app. If you need product analytics inside the app, pick a vendor that signs a BAA and send events without patient ids or field values.
findings.subject: Google Analytics

findings.title: Health data written to function logs

cwe.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

findings.whyItMatters: Everything an edge function prints goes to the Supabase logs, which anyone with dashboard access can read and which are kept outside your tables, policies and audit trail. Logged patient records are health data in a place nobody reviews.
findings.fix: Log ids and outcomes only (`appointment ${id}: reminder sent`), never whole rows or fields from health tables.
findings.subject: logs (supabase/functions/send-reminder/index.ts)

findings.title: No audit trail for changes to health records
findings.evidence: No audit trail of changes to the tables with health data: `public.appointments`, `public.patients`, `public.prescriptions`.
findings.snippet:
1 | create table public.appointments (
   2 |   id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
   3 |   patient_id uuid not null references public.patients (id) on delete cascade,
   4 |   scheduled_at timestamptz not null,
findings.whyItMatters: The HIPAA Security Rule asks for audit controls: a record of who created, changed or deleted health data and when. Nothing in the migrations writes one, so after a mistake or a breach there is no way to tell who did what.
findings.fix: Add an append-only audit table that a trigger fills on every insert, update and delete of the health tables, with the user id from `auth.uid()`, and that nobody, including the app, can update or delete.
findings.subject: phi-audit-log

patch.summary: Adds public.phi_audit_log and a trigger on public.appointments, public.patients, public.prescriptions that records who inserted, changed or deleted which row, and when. The log keeps ids only, no health data, and nobody can update or delete it.
caveats: Postgres cannot log reads with a trigger. If you must record who viewed a record, turn on the pgaudit extension or log reads in a server function.

Changes made with the service role key (edge functions, scripts) are logged with actor_role service_role and no user id: pass the user's JWT to the client in edge functions when you want the person recorded.
Reading the log needs the service role (or a dashboard SQL query). Add a policy for an admin role if staff must see it in the app.

findings.title: Public storage bucket

cwe.name: Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties

findings.evidence: Storage bucket `clinic-logos` is public: anyone with a file's URL can download it. The bucket's name says it holds site content (logos, CMS images). Confirm nothing uploaded by users or patients ever lands in it.
findings.snippet:
10 | insert into storage.buckets (id, name, public)
  11 | values ('clinic-logos', 'clinic-logos', true);
findings.whyItMatters: Files in a public bucket open for anyone with the link. When a select policy on storage.objects also lets anyone list the bucket, the links are no secret either: anyone can download every file.
findings.fix: Make the bucket private, drop the open select policy, and hand out short-lived signed URLs from the server after checking who is asking.
findings.subject: clinic-logos

findings.title: Policy lets everyone through (using true)
findings.evidence: Policy "Anyone can read clinic locations" on `public.clinic_locations` (select) lets anyone (signed in or not) read every row.
findings.snippet:
11 | create policy "Anyone can read clinic locations"
  12 |   on public.clinic_locations for select
  13 |   to anon, authenticated
  14 |   using (true);
findings.whyItMatters: A policy with `using (true)` or `with check (true)` allows the action for every caller, including visitors who are not signed in. If the table holds anything private, it is public.
findings.fix: Replace the policy with one that compares `auth.uid()` to the owner column, and limit it to the `authenticated` role.

controls.control: Sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with Supabase
controls.detail: Needs the Team plan or above and the HIPAA add-on (request form in the Supabase docs).

controls.control: Mark the project as High Compliance and fix what the Security Advisor raises
MFA on every Supabase account, enforced for the organization

controls.detail: Database settings: allow only the addresses that need direct database access.
Supabase sets log_connections off by default for new projects; the Security Advisor warns when it is off.

controls.control: Encryption as the HIPAA Security Rule asks
controls.detail: Supabase encrypts data at rest and in transit; consider encrypting the most sensitive columns in the app as well.

controls.control: No PHI in public Storage buckets
controls.detail: Public buckets that hold health files: lab-results.

controls.control: Never transfer the project to an organization without the HIPAA add-on
A BAA with every other vendor that receives PHI (beyond the Supabase list)
controls.detail: The code sends health data to, or loads on health pages: Google Analytics, PostHog, Resend, OpenAI. Each needs a signed BAA or has to stop getting the data.

controls.control: Audit trail of who changed health records (HIPAA Security Rule, audit controls)
controls.detail: No audit trigger on public.appointments, public.patients, public.prescriptions.

notChecked: The deployed site: no URL was given, so HTTPS, security headers, cookies and the built JavaScript bundles were not checked.
Business logic and authorization inside your own API routes, server actions and edge functions (beyond the Stripe webhook).
Rate limiting, abuse and brute-force protection, email/auth settings in the Supabase dashboard.
Dependencies with known CVEs: npm audit was turned off for this run.

The live database: policies or grants changed in the Supabase dashboard and not saved as migrations are invisible to a repo scan. The RLS probe runs your migrations in a local Postgres, not against your project.
Manual penetration testing: every finding here comes from automated scanners and a local probe, and nothing was tried against your running app.

HIPAA compliance as a whole: this report finds technical gaps in the code. Compliance also needs a risk analysis, policies, staff training and signed agreements, and only a qualified person can sign it off. Nothing here is legal advice.
Health data under column names the map does not know: PHI is found by names such as diagnosis, date_of_birth or mrn. Check the PHI map against your schema.
Who reads health records: Postgres triggers log changes, not reads. Read logging needs pgaudit or server-side code.
